title: The Dragon Who Lost His Shine
markdown:
The Dragon’s Tooth range groaned under a banshee howl, ice and stone clawing at the sky. Ogre Tolliver, broad as a boulder, shouldered his pack. Beside him, Lumen, an owl with amber eyes, missed nothing.

“All under control,” Tolliver rumbled.

A smaller creature of nervousness still fluttered in him. He was guiding Bartholomew, a fussy merchant who must not be allowed to notice the flutter. Wing to shoulder, they went. That was the first time Tolliver thought it, and he did not say it aloud.

They plunged into a valley of emerald gloom. A vast shadow blotted the sun. High above, Ignis, the dragon librarian, circled with breathtaking grace. Scales like a thousand emeralds. Temperament like a dropped teacup. Bartholomew’s eyes went wide as saucers.

“A dragon,” he shrieked, finger trembling.

Ignis recoiled, spiraling down.

“Hush. Hush, you earsplitting creature,” she hissed, crackling twigs. Bartholomew squeaked and dove behind Tolliver.

Tolliver bowed. “My apologies, esteemed Ignis. My guest is prone to sudden exclamations.”

Ignis huffed smoke. “Exclamations is charitable.” She launched upward, muttering about indignity.

Wing to shoulder, Tolliver thought again, and this time Lumen’s feathers brushed his ear as if in agreement.

Their path led to a cliffside marketplace, starlight herbs and sun-gem trinkets, nervous whispers instead of haggling.

“Emberscale is beside himself,” a gnome lamented to a fae. “The Grand Fire-Dance is ruined.”

Emberscale, the valley’s most venerable dragon, was known for quiet majesty. His heart, people said, was delicate as frost. Bartholomew wrung his hands.

“Oh dear. A dragon in a sulk. What will become of us?”

Tolliver watched a small bird chirping near glowing fungi, then the anxious faces.

“He is not angry. He is deeply disappointed.”

Bartholomew blinked. “Disappointed? How can you tell, you lummox? He looks as if he’ll unleash inferno.”

“It’s his tail,” Tolliver said. “Not fury. Sadness.”

They ascended to Emberscale’s aerie, Lumen a silent weight. The entrance gaped, dark and somber. Bartholomew followed at a respectful, which is to say cowardly, distance. Tolliver settled, a patient sentinel.

Then Lumen began to sing. No words. Melody woven from rustling leaves, trickling snowmelt, sighing wind. Quiet dawn. Glittering stars. Strength in stillness. Tolliver did not speak. He sat. The pack stayed on. The howl of the range went on without them. That was the work: waiting while a song did what a speech would only bruise.

A colossal scaled head emerged. Emberscale’s eyes, usually molten gold, were clouded.

“Why disturb my solitude? My scales have lost their lustre. My fire dwindles. The world is too loud, and I feel a shadow.”

Tolliver’s voice was a balm, not a lecture. “Your scales still hold sunlight’s memory. Your fire still knows hearth-warmth. We do not need your roar. We need you as you are.”

Lumen landed nearby, trilled, and nudged a fallen feather, a soft down plume, toward the dragon. Emberscale gazed at the feather, at Tolliver’s steady eyes, at the owl. A flicker. He nudged the feather back. Bartholomew whispered, “Well done,” which was, for Bartholomew, almost a hymn. The market below exhaled.

That evening the Grand Fire-Dance began: silent flames across the sky, Emberscale’s grace restored enough to be seen. Tolliver prepared to guide Bartholomew down. At the valley’s edge, stars pricking indigo, Lumen ruffled his feathers.

“My journey with you has been rewarding. But my nest lies here, among these peaks.” Amber eyes. “I shall remain.”

Wing to shoulder, Tolliver thought a third time, and this time it hurt in a clean way. He nodded.

“Then stay, Lumen. You’ll always find welcome.”

The owl took flight. Tolliver watched until the dark took the pale of him. Bartholomew, for once, did not remark. The Fire-Dance went on without commentary, which was the kindest thing the night did. Tolliver turned toward the path home with a merchant and no owl, and the pack felt the same weight, and also did not.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, highland fantasy adventure for teens
